To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) SKMBs and BMNCs have demonstrated efficacy in animal models of myocardial ischemia and infarction, respectively; (2) SKMBs are more likely to engraft and survive in the infarcted myocardium, whereas BMNCs are more likely than SKMBs to differentiate into cardiac cells; (3) both cell types have shown safety in clinical trials; (4) SKMBs have been associated with a higher rate of arrhythmias

(i) SKMB transplantation in a porcine model of myocardial infarction is safe and effective, (ii) SKMB transplantation results in a significant reduction in LV end-systolic volumes and a trend towards a reduction in LV end-diastolic volumes, (iii) SKMB transplantation improves regional systolic function, (iv) SKMB transplantation is associated with an increase in the number of viable myocytes, (v) SKMB transplantation increases the density of capillaries

(1) intracoronary injection of BMNCs and intramyocardial injection of SKMBs are safe and feasible; (2) the clinical benefit of these therapies is modest, and (3) further studies are needed to better understand their mechanisms of action and to optimize their delivery and clinical outcome measures
In summary, our research is concerned with

the development of cell-based therapies for the treatment of cardiovascular disease, with a focus on the identification of cell populations that can be used for cardiac repair and the definition of the mechanisms by which these cells exert their beneficial effects.
the development and application of novel therapeutic concepts for the treatment of cardiovascular diseases.
the development of new therapies for cardiovascular disease.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the field of cell therapy for CVD is in its infancy and requires further investigation.
both cell types are effective in treating patients with ischemic CVD, and that the choice of one over the other is not yet possible.
both cell types have shown promise, but that more work remains to be done to optimize the use of these cells in the clinic.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the cell therapy for heart disease is a promising new treatment modality.
we have demonstrated that skeletal myoblast cells and bone marrow mononuclear cells can be used to treat heart failure patients.
cell-based therapy is a promising and potentially effective approach to treat and prevent CVD.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the most effective cell therapy for the failing heart is one that can deliver the highest possible dose of viable cells to the myocardium in the most efficient way possible.
the field is still at a very preliminary stage.
there is a clear need to define the most suitable cell types for myocardial repair and to determine the optimal delivery methods.
